questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $m\geq n$, and rows $\boldsymbol{a}_1^{\top},\dots,\boldsymbol{a}_m^{\top}$. Which condition on a point $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$ is equivalent to $\boldsymbol{p}$ being an extreme point of $V$?
options: $\boldsymbol{p}$ is the only solution of the full system $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}$ of all $m$ equations.
$\boldsymbol{p}$ solves $n$ of the equations $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b_i$, whether or not they have other common solutions.
For some $n$ rows, $\boldsymbol{p}$ is the only common solution of the equations $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b_i$ of these rows.
$\boldsymbol{p}$ satisfies at least one equation $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b_i$, so it lies on a boundary hyperplane of $V$.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$ with $m\geq n$, and let $\boldsymbol{q}$ be the unique solution of $n$ equations $\boldsymbol{a}_{r_j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b_{r_j}$ with linearly independent rows. What must still be checked to conclude $\boldsymbol{q}\in\operatorname{Ext}(V)$?
options: That $\boldsymbol{q}$ also satisfies the other inequalities, so $\boldsymbol{q}\in V$.
Nothing more: the unique solution of $n$ independent equations is always extreme.
That no further row binds at $\boldsymbol{q}$, so that exactly $n$ rows are binding.
That $V$ is bounded, because only bounded sets can have extreme points.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $m\geq n$. Which argument explains why $V$ has only finitely many extreme points?
options: $V$ is closed and bounded, and a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ has only finitely many boundary points.
Each extreme point is the unique solution of $n$ of the $m$ boundary equations, and there are $\binom{m}{n}$ such choices.
Each extreme point lies on a hyperplane $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b_i$, and there are only $m$ such hyperplanes.
Any two hyperplanes $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b_i$ meet in at most one point, giving at most $\binom{m}{2}$ extreme points.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$, $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$ and $I(\boldsymbol{p})=\{i\colon\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}=b_i\}$. In the criterion '$\boldsymbol{p}$ is extreme if and only if $\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{A}_{I(\boldsymbol{p})})=n$', which matrix is $\boldsymbol{A}_{I(\boldsymbol{p})}$?
options: The matrix of the rows $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}$ of $\boldsymbol{A}$ with $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}<b_i$.
The matrix of the columns of $\boldsymbol{A}$ whose index $j$ satisfies $p_j\neq0$.
The square $n\times n$ matrix of the first $n$ rows of $\boldsymbol{A}$ that bind at $\boldsymbol{p}$.
The matrix of all rows $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}$ of $\boldsymbol{A}$ with $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}=b_i$.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{A})<n$. Which statement about $V$ is correct?
options: $V$ has no extreme points, even when $V$ itself is nonempty.
$V$ is empty, since the inequalities $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$ then have no solution.
$V$ has extreme points only where more than $n$ rows of $\boldsymbol{A}$ bind.
$V$ has infinitely many extreme points, as $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}$ has many solutions.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+x_2\leq5,\ 2x_1-x_2\leq4,\ -x_1+3x_2\leq9,\ -x_2\leq0\}$, with rows numbered $1$ to $4$ in this order, and $\boldsymbol{p}=(3,2)\in V$. What is the binding index set $I(\boldsymbol{p})$, and is $\boldsymbol{p}$ an extreme point of $V$?
options: $I(\boldsymbol{p})=\{3,4\}$, and $\boldsymbol{p}$ is not an extreme point.
$I(\boldsymbol{p})=\{1,2\}$, and $\boldsymbol{p}$ is an extreme point.
$I(\boldsymbol{p})=\{1,2,3,4\}$, and $\boldsymbol{p}$ is an extreme point.
$I(\boldsymbol{p})=\{1,2\}$, but $\boldsymbol{p}$ is not extreme as rows $3$, $4$ do not bind.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_1+x_2+x_3\leq4,\ -x_1-x_2-x_3\leq-4,\ -x_1\leq0,\ -x_2\leq0,\ -x_3\leq0\}$, so the first two rows encode $x_1+x_2+x_3=4$. At $\boldsymbol{p}=(2,2,0)$, how many rows bind, what is the rank of the binding rows, and is $\boldsymbol{p}$ extreme?
options: Three rows bind with rank $3$, so $\boldsymbol{p}$ is an extreme point.
One row binds ($-x_3\leq0$) with rank $1$, so $\boldsymbol{p}$ is not extreme.
Three rows bind with rank $2$, so $\boldsymbol{p}$ is not an extreme point.
Three rows bind with rank $2$, and as $3=n$ rows bind, $\boldsymbol{p}$ is extreme.

questions.question: Each set below is a polyhedral convex set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ given by its inequalities. Which of these sets has no extreme points?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon x_1\leq1,\ x_2\leq1\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon x_1+x_2\leq1,\ x_1-x_2\leq1\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon -x_2\leq0,\ x_2\leq1,\ x_1\leq0\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon x_1-x_2\leq1,\ -x_1+x_2\leq1\}$

questions.question: The cube $[0,1]^3$ is written as $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$ with $n=3$ and the $m=6$ rows $x_j\leq1$ and $-x_j\leq0$ for $j=1,2,3$. What upper bound $\binom{m}{n}$ does the count of $n$-row subsystems give, and how many extreme points does the cube actually have?
options: Bound $\binom{6}{3}=20$; the cube has $8$ extreme points.
Bound $\binom{6}{3}=20$; the cube has $20$ extreme points.
Bound $6\cdot5\cdot4=120$; the cube has $48$ extreme points.
Bound $\binom{6}{2}=15$; the cube has $12$ extreme points.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_1+x_2+x_3\leq6,\ -x_1\leq0,\ -x_2\leq0,\ -x_3\leq0\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(0,0,3)$. Which conclusion about $\boldsymbol{p}$ is correct?
options: Extreme: the two binding rows $-x_1\leq0$ and $-x_2\leq0$ are linearly independent.
Extreme: $\boldsymbol{p}$ cannot move in the $-x_1$ or the $-x_2$ direction without leaving $V$.
Not extreme: the binding rows $-x_1\leq0$ and $-x_2\leq0$ have rank $2<3$.
Not extreme: no row binds at $\boldsymbol{p}$, so $\boldsymbol{p}$ is an interior point of $V$.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$, $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$, and $\boldsymbol{d}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ with $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}=0$ for every row $i$ that binds at $\boldsymbol{p}$. Why is $\boldsymbol{p}\pm\varepsilon\boldsymbol{d}\in V$ for small enough $\varepsilon>0$?
options: All $m$ rows satisfy $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}=0$, so $\boldsymbol{p}\pm\varepsilon\boldsymbol{d}$ meets every inequality as $\boldsymbol{p}$ does, for any $\varepsilon$.
$V$ is unbounded in the direction $\boldsymbol{d}$, so $\boldsymbol{p}\pm\varepsilon\boldsymbol{d}\in V$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.
The nonbinding rows can be deleted without changing $V$, so only the binding rows have to be checked.
Binding rows keep equality at $\boldsymbol{p}\pm\varepsilon\boldsymbol{d}$, and the finitely many nonbinding rows have slack at $\boldsymbol{p}$ that a small step keeps.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$, and let row $i$ bind at $\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{y}$, where $\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in V$ and $\lambda\in(0,1)$. Which argument shows $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=b_i$?
options: By linearity alone, $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}$, as $\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}$ both lie in the same set $V$.
$b_i$ is a weighted average, with positive weights, of $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i$ and $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\leq b_i$, so neither is below $b_i$.
$\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}$ are extreme points of $V$, so they satisfy the same binding equations as the point $\boldsymbol{p}$.
$\boldsymbol{p}$ is an extreme point of $V$, so $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{p}$ and the binding equation carries over to both.

questions.question: Which argument shows that the closed unit disc $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1^2+x_2^2\leq1\}$ is not a polyhedral convex set $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$ for any $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times2}$, $\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^m$?
options: A polyhedral set has finitely many extreme points, while the disc has infinitely many.
A polyhedral set is always unbounded, but the closed unit disc is bounded.
A polyhedral set with $\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{A})=2$ has extreme points, while the disc has none.
A polyhedral set has at most $\binom{m}{2}$ boundary points, but the disc has infinitely many.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_2\leq3,\ -x_2\leq1,\ x_1+x_2\leq4,\ x_1-x_2\leq3\}$. How many extreme points does $V$ have?

For a real parameter $t$, let $V_t=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+x_2\leq2,\ tx_1+2x_2\leq t+2,\ -x_1\leq0\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,1)$, which lies in $V_t$ for every $t$. For which $t$ is $\boldsymbol{p}$ an extreme point of $V_t$?
options: For every real $t$
Only for $t=2$
For every $t\neq-2$
For every $t\neq2$

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_1+x_2\leq2,\ x_2+x_3\leq2,\ x_1+2x_2+x_3\leq4,\ -x_1\leq0,\ -x_2\leq0,\ -x_3\leq0\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,1,1)$. For which $\boldsymbol{d}$ do both $\boldsymbol{p}+\boldsymbol{d}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}-\boldsymbol{d}$ lie in $V$, showing $\boldsymbol{p}$ is not extreme?
options: $\boldsymbol{d}=(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},0)$
$\boldsymbol{d}=(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$
$\boldsymbol{d}=(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2},0)$
$\boldsymbol{d}=(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$ with $m\geq n$, and $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$. How is the condition 'at least $n$ of the $m$ inequalities bind at $\boldsymbol{p}$' related to $\boldsymbol{p}$ being an extreme point of $V$?
options: It is necessary but not sufficient for $\boldsymbol{p}$ to be extreme.
It is sufficient but not necessary for $\boldsymbol{p}$ to be extreme.
It is necessary and sufficient for $\boldsymbol{p}$ to be extreme.
It is neither necessary nor sufficient for $\boldsymbol{p}$ to be extreme.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $m\geq n$. An extra inequality $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq d$ that holds at every point of $V$ is added, so the $m+1$ rows describe the same set $V$. Which statement is correct?
options: $\operatorname{Ext}(V)$ gains the points of $V$ where $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=d$ meets $n-1$ of the old boundary hyperplanes.
An extreme point at which $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq d$ binds stops being extreme, since more than $n$ rows bind.
$\operatorname{Ext}(V)$ and the bound $\binom{m}{n}$ both stay the same, since a redundant row never binds.
$\operatorname{Ext}(V)$ stays the same, although the bound on its size grows from $\binom{m}{n}$ to $\binom{m+1}{n}$.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_1\leq2,\ x_2\leq2,\ x_1+x_2\leq4,\ x_1+x_2+x_3\leq5,\ -x_3\leq0\}$, with rows numbered $1$ to $5$ in this order, and $\boldsymbol{p}=(2,2,1)\in V$. Which choice of rows $r_1,r_2,r_3$ makes $\boldsymbol{p}$ the unique common solution of the equations $\boldsymbol{a}_{r_j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b_{r_j}$, $j=1,2,3$?
options: Rows $1$, $2$ and $3$
Rows $1$, $2$ and $5$
Rows $1$, $2$ and $4$
None, since four rows bind at $\boldsymbol{p}$

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon 0\leq x_3\leq\min(x_1,\,x_2,\,2-x_1,\,2-x_2)\}$, described by the $m=5$ inequalities $-x_3\leq0$, $x_3-x_1\leq0$, $x_3-x_2\leq0$, $x_1+x_3\leq2$, $x_2+x_3\leq2$. How many extreme points does $V$ have?
